description: Subject-Verb Agreement question bank derived from FDA & SDA Competitive Examination Notes. Covers all rules, exceptions, and exam traps.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the core principle of subject-verb agreement?

options.A: A finite verb agrees with the nearest noun
options.B: A finite verb agrees with its subject in grammatical number and person
options.C: A verb agrees with the object of the sentence
options.D: A verb agrees with the noun placed immediately before it

questions.explanation: A finite verb normally agrees with its subject in grammatical number and person—not simply with the nearest noun or the noun placed immediately before the verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a subject in a clause?

options.A: The word that expresses an action
options.B: The word or group of words that the clause is about and that controls agreement on the finite verb
options.C: The word that receives the action of the verb
options.D: The word that describes the verb

questions.explanation: The subject is the word or group of words that the clause is about and that controls agreement on the finite verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a finite verb?

options.A: A verb form that shows tense and/or agreement and can function as the main verb of an independent clause
options.B: A verb form that does not change with tense
options.D: A verb form that functions only as an adjective

questions.explanation: A finite verb is a verb form that shows tense and/or agreement and can function as the main verb of an independent clause: 'She works'; 'They were waiting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a singular subject?

options.A: A subject referring grammatically to more than one person or thing
options.B: A subject referring grammatically to one person, thing, place, idea or unit
options.C: A subject that always takes a plural verb
options.D: A subject that is always a proper noun

questions.explanation: A singular subject refers grammatically to one person, thing, place, idea or unit: 'The student studies.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a plural subject?

options.A: A subject referring grammatically to one unit
options.B: A subject referring grammatically to more than one
options.C: A subject that always takes a singular verb
options.D: A subject that is always a collective noun

questions.explanation: A plural subject refers grammatically to more than one: 'The students study.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does the verb agree with the subject or the object?
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject, not the object: 'The boy likes apples,' not 'The boy like apples.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does a verb automatically agree with the nearest noun?

options.B: No, it agrees with the grammatical subject

questions.explanation: A verb does not automatically agree with the nearest noun. It agrees with the grammatical subject. Ignore intervening nouns in phrases such as 'The box of books is heavy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between grammatical number and real-world number?

options.A: Grammatical number is the singular/plural form assigned by grammar; real-world quantity is how many people or things are involved
options.B: Grammatical number always matches real-world quantity
options.D: Grammatical number only applies to verbs

questions.explanation: Grammatical number is the singular/plural form assigned by grammar; real-world quantity is how many people or things are involved. Some nouns that refer to groups or multiple items take singular grammar.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb form is used with he, she, it or a singular noun in the simple present?

options.B: The main verb generally takes -s or -es

questions.explanation: The main verb generally takes -s or -es: 'She reads'; 'The child watches.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb form is used with I, you, we, they and plural nouns in the simple present?
questions.explanation: The base form (V1) is used: 'I read'; 'They watch.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does the verb 'do' change in the simple present?

options.A: Does is used with he/she/it and singular nouns; do is used with I/you/we/they and plural nouns
options.B: Do is used with he/she/it; does is used with plural nouns
options.C: Do is used with all subjects
options.D: Does is used with all subjects

questions.explanation: Does is used with he/she/it and singular nouns; do is used with I/you/we/they and plural nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does the verb 'have' change in the simple present?

options.A: Has is used with he/she/it and singular nouns; have is used with I/you/we/they and plural nouns
options.B: Have is used with he/she/it; has is used with plural nouns
options.C: Has is used with all subjects
options.D: Have is used with all subjects

questions.explanation: Has is used with he/she/it and singular nouns; have is used with I/you/we/they and plural nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does the verb 'be' change in the present tense?

options.A: Am is used with I; is with he/she/it and singular nouns; are with you/we/they and plural nouns
options.B: Is is used with I; am with you; are with he/she/it
options.C: Are is used with all subjects
options.D: Am is used with all subjects

questions.explanation: Am is used with I; is with he/she/it and singular nouns; are with you/we/they and plural nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does the verb 'be' change in the past tense?

options.A: Was is used with I/he/she/it and singular nouns; were is used with you/we/they and plural nouns
options.B: Were is used with I/he/she/it; was is used with plural nouns
options.C: Was is used with all subjects
options.D: Were is used with all subjects

questions.explanation: Was is used with I/he/she/it and singular nouns; were is used with you/we/they and plural nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does the modal verb change according to the subject?

options.A: Yes, modals change for singular and plural subjects
options.B: No, modals such as can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will and would do not change for singular or plural subjects

questions.explanation: Modals such as can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will and would do not change for singular or plural subjects: 'She can swim'; 'They can swim.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is generally used when two singular subjects are joined by 'and'?
questions.explanation: A plural verb is used: 'Ravi and Rani are friends.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule when two nouns joined by 'and' refer to one person or one combined idea?

options.A: A plural verb must always be used
options.B: A singular verb may be used when the words form one unit, one dish, one title or one concept

questions.explanation: A singular verb may be used when the words form one unit, one dish, one title or one concept: 'Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.' Context determines whether they are one unit or two separate subjects.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used when 'each' or 'every' precedes nouns joined by 'and'?

options.B: A singular verb is generally used when each/every distributes the subjects individually

questions.explanation: A singular verb is generally used when each/every distributes the subjects individually: 'Every boy and every girl is invited.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens when two singular nouns joined by 'and' refer to the same person?

options.A: A plural verb is always used
options.B: A singular verb is used when both descriptions identify one person

questions.explanation: A singular verb is used when both descriptions identify one person: 'The poet and novelist is attending.' The article can help show whether one or two people are meant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Compare 'The poet and the novelist are here' with 'The poet and novelist is here.' What is the difference?

options.A: The first refers to two people; the second can refer to one person who is both a poet and a novelist
options.D: The first refers to one person; the second refers to two people

questions.explanation: The first normally refers to two people; the second can refer to one person who is both a poet and a novelist.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with two subjects joined by 'and' but preceded by 'each'?
questions.explanation: Usually singular: 'Each man and each woman has a vote.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor' when the subjects differ in number or person?

options.A: The verb always agrees with the first subject
options.B: The verb generally agrees with the subject nearer to it

questions.explanation: When the subjects differ in number or person, the verb generally agrees with the subject nearer to it: 'Neither the manager nor the workers are available.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the proximity rule?

options.A: The verb agrees with the subject farthest from it
options.B: With either...or, neither...nor, or...or and nor...nor constructions, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject
options.C: The verb always agrees with the first subject
options.D: The verb always agrees with the subject in the object position

questions.explanation: With either...or, neither...nor, or...or and nor...nor constructions, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence: 'Neither the teachers nor the principal ___ present.'
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, principal, is singular, so 'is' is used.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers ___ present.'
questions.explanation: The nearer subject, teachers, is plural, so 'are' is used.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the preferred way to avoid an awkward agreement construction with either/or and neither/nor?

options.B: Rewrite the sentence so that the subjects have the same number or use a plural construction where appropriate

questions.explanation: Rewrite the sentence so that the subjects have the same number or use a plural construction where appropriate: 'The manager and the workers are unavailable.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used when both alternatives are singular and joined by 'either...or'?
questions.explanation: A singular verb is used: 'Either Ravi or Rani is responsible.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used when both alternatives are plural and joined by 'either...or'?
questions.explanation: A plural verb is used: 'Either the boys or the girls are responsible.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does 'as well as' make a singular subject plural?

options.B: No, the verb agrees with the main subject

questions.explanation: No. The verb agrees with the main subject: 'The captain, as well as the players, is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'along with'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the noun after 'along with'
options.B: The verb agrees with the first/main subject

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the first/main subject: 'The principal, along with the teachers, is attending.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'together with'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the noun after 'together with'
options.B: The verb agrees with the main subject

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the main subject: 'The students, together with their teacher, are going.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'in addition to'?

options.A: The phrase does not normally change the number of the main subject
options.B: The phrase makes the subject plural
options.C: The verb agrees with the noun after 'in addition to'

questions.explanation: The phrase does not normally change the number of the main subject: 'The clerk, in addition to two assistants, is present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'accompanied by'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the noun after 'accompanied by'
options.B: The verb agrees with the main subject

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the main subject: 'The officer, accompanied by two guards, was arriving.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'rather than' and 'except'?

options.A: These expressions do not automatically create a compound subject; identify the grammatical subject and make the verb agree with it
options.B: These expressions always make the subject plural
options.C: These expressions always make the subject singular
options.D: These expressions require a modal verb

questions.explanation: These expressions do not automatically create a compound subject; identify the grammatical subject and make the verb agree with it.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which indefinite pronouns normally take singular verbs?

options.B: Each, either, neither, everyone, everybody, everything, someone, somebody, something, anyone, anybody, anything, no one, nobody, nothing, one and much

questions.explanation: Each, either, neither, everyone, everybody, everything, someone, somebody, something, anyone, anybody, anything, no one, nobody, nothing, one and much normally take singular verbs: 'Everyone is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'each'?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Each has a ticket.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'everyone' and 'everybody'?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Everyone knows the answer'; 'Everybody is welcome.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'someone', 'somebody', 'anyone' and 'nobody'?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Someone is waiting'; 'Nobody knows.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'either' and 'neither' when they stand alone as subjects?
questions.explanation: Singular in standard formal agreement: 'Either is acceptable'; 'Neither is correct.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'one of...'?

options.A: Plural, because of the plural noun after 'of'
options.B: Singular, because the main subject is 'one'

questions.explanation: The main subject is one, so use a singular verb: 'One of the students is absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'each of...'?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Each of the candidates has an identity card.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'either of...' and 'neither of...' in formal exam grammar?
questions.explanation: Formal exam grammar generally expects a singular verb: 'Neither of the answers is correct.' Informal usage may vary in some contexts.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'many a'?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Many a student has made this mistake.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which indefinite pronouns normally take plural verbs?
questions.explanation: Both, few, many and several normally take plural verbs: 'Both are correct'; 'Several have applied.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'both'?
questions.explanation: Plural: 'Both are present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'few', 'many' and 'several'?
questions.explanation: Plural: 'Few know the answer'; 'Many were selected'; 'Several have arrived.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'all', 'some', 'most', 'any' and 'none'?

options.C: It depends on the noun or meaning

questions.explanation: It depends on the noun or meaning: 'Some of the water is missing' (uncountable); 'Some of the students are absent' (plural countable).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does 'none' always take a singular verb?

options.B: No, both singular and plural agreement occur depending on meaning and construction
options.D: No, it always takes a plural verb

questions.explanation: None can mean not one or not any. Both singular and plural agreement occur depending on meaning and construction: 'None of the money is missing'; 'None of the students are ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'half', 'part', 'a lot', 'plenty' and 'the rest'?

options.C: The verb generally agrees with the noun in the of-phrase

questions.explanation: The verb generally agrees with the noun in the of-phrase: 'Half of the cake is gone'; 'Half of the students are absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for percentages and fractions?

options.C: The verb agrees with the noun after 'of'

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the noun after of: 'Sixty per cent of the land is fertile'; 'Sixty per cent of the workers are women.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'a number of'?

options.A: A number of + plural noun normally takes a singular verb
options.B: A number of + plural noun normally takes a plural verb
options.C: A number of + singular noun takes a plural verb
options.D: A number of always takes a modal verb

questions.explanation: A number of + plural noun normally takes a plural verb: 'A number of applicants are waiting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'the number of'?

options.A: The number of + plural noun takes a plural verb
options.B: The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb because the subject is 'number'
options.C: The number of + singular noun takes a plural verb
options.D: The number of always takes a modal verb

questions.explanation: The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb because the subject is number: 'The number of applicants is increasing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'a great many of'?

options.A: It normally takes a singular verb
options.B: It normally takes a plural verb
options.C: It always takes a modal verb

questions.explanation: It normally takes a plural verb: 'A great many of the houses were damaged.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'plenty of'?

options.A: It always takes a singular verb
options.B: It always takes a plural verb
options.C: It depends on the noun: 'Plenty of time is available'; 'Plenty of seats are available'
options.D: It always takes a modal verb

questions.explanation: It depends on the noun: 'Plenty of time is available'; 'Plenty of seats are available.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a collective noun?

options.A: A plural noun referring to individuals
options.B: A singular noun referring to a group of people, animals or things considered as a unit
options.C: A noun that cannot be counted
options.D: A noun that only appears in plural form

questions.explanation: A collective noun is a singular noun referring to a group of people, animals or things considered as a unit: team, committee, family, audience, jury, staff, class and crowd.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with a collective noun when the group acts as one unit?
questions.explanation: A singular verb is used: 'The committee has submitted its report.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a collective noun take a plural verb?

options.B: Yes, especially in British English when members are considered individually

questions.explanation: Yes, especially in British English when members are considered individually: 'The committee are divided in their opinions.' The singular/plural choice depends on meaning and dialect.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What should be used in a typical objective examination if the group is treated as one unit?
questions.explanation: A singular verb should be used: 'The team is playing well.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'The family is large' and 'The family are arguing among themselves'?

options.A: 'Is' treats the family as one unit; 'are' focuses on individual members
options.B: 'Is' focuses on individuals; 'are' treats the family as one unit
options.C: Both treat the family as one unit

questions.explanation: Is treats the family as one unit; are focuses on individual members. British English permits this notional plural agreement more readily.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Are 'police', 'cattle' and 'people' normally singular or plural in agreement?
questions.explanation: They are plural in standard usage: 'The police are investigating'; 'Cattle are grazing'; 'People are waiting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'the police'?
questions.explanation: Plural: 'The police have arrived.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'cattle'?
questions.explanation: Plural: 'The cattle are grazing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'the public'?

options.C: It can be singular when treated as a collective body or plural when individuals are emphasised

questions.explanation: It can be singular when treated as a collective body ('The public is concerned') or plural when individuals are emphasised in some varieties and contexts. Follow the sentence meaning and exam convention.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with uncountable nouns?
questions.explanation: A singular verb is used: 'Information is useful'; 'Furniture is expensive'; 'Advice is valuable.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a common uncountable noun that takes a singular verb?
questions.explanation: Information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, knowledge, traffic, bread, water, rice, milk, money and homework are common uncountable nouns that take singular verbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'news' singular or plural?
questions.explanation: News is grammatically singular: 'The news is encouraging.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'mathematics' singular or plural when referring to the subject?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Mathematics is difficult.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'physics' singular or plural when referring to the academic subject?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Physics is interesting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'measles' singular or plural?
questions.explanation: The disease name measles is generally singular: 'Measles is contagious.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'a piece of information' singular or plural?

options.B: Singular; two pieces of information is plural because 'piece' is the count noun

questions.explanation: One piece of information is singular; two pieces of information is plural because piece is the count noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'trousers', 'scissors', 'spectacles' and 'binoculars'?
questions.explanation: Plural: 'These scissors are sharp'; 'My trousers are new.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How can a singular verb be used with 'scissors' or 'trousers'?

options.A: When preceded by 'a pair of', the grammatical subject 'pair' is singular
options.B: When preceded by 'the', the subject becomes singular
options.C: When preceded by 'these', the subject becomes singular

questions.explanation: When preceded by 'a pair of', the grammatical subject pair is singular: 'A pair of scissors is on the table.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'goods', 'belongings', 'surroundings' and 'earnings'?
questions.explanation: Normally plural: 'The goods are damaged'; 'Her earnings are increasing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'people' and 'police'?
questions.explanation: Plural: 'The people are waiting'; 'The police are here.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'sheep', 'deer' and 'fish'?

options.C: The noun has the same singular and plural form, but the verb depends on number

questions.explanation: The noun has the same singular and plural form, but the verb depends on number: 'The sheep is ill'; 'The sheep are grazing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'series' and 'species'?

options.C: They can be singular or plural depending on meaning

questions.explanation: They can be singular or plural depending on meaning: 'This species is rare'; 'Several species are endangered.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'means'?

options.C: It can be singular or plural depending on meaning

questions.explanation: It can be singular or plural: 'A means of transport is available'; 'Several means are available.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'headquarters'?

options.C: It can be singular or plural depending on meaning

questions.explanation: It can be singular or plural depending on meaning: 'The headquarters is in Bengaluru'; 'Several headquarters are listed.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with subjects such as 'mathematics', 'economics', 'politics' and 'physics'?

options.B: Usually singular when they refer to academic subjects or fields

questions.explanation: Usually singular when they refer to academic subjects or fields: 'Economics is a social science.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with names of books, films, organisations or titles that look plural?

options.B: Usually singular when the title names one work or entity

questions.explanation: Usually singular when the title names one work or entity: 'Gulliver's Travels is a novel.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'the United States' when it names one country?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'The United States is a federal republic.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'the United Nations' when it names one organisation?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'The United Nations is an international organisation.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with a sum of money considered as one amount?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Five hundred rupees is enough.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with a period of time considered as one unit?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Ten years is a long time.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with a distance considered as one unit?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Twenty kilometres is a long distance.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with a weight or measurement considered as one unit?
questions.explanation: Singular: 'Five kilograms is too heavy for this parcel.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When can amounts and measurements take plural verbs?

options.B: When the individual units or items are emphasised

questions.explanation: When the individual units or items are emphasised: 'The ten rupees were in separate coins'; 'The five kilometres were difficult to cover.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with arithmetic expressions such as 'two and two'?

options.A: Usually plural when the result is treated as one
options.B: Usually singular when the result or sum is treated as one

questions.explanation: Usually singular when the result or sum is treated as one: 'Two and two is four.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an intervening phrase?

options.A: A phrase that changes the subject-verb agreement
options.B: A phrase placed between the subject and verb that may contain another noun but does not usually change subject-verb agreement
options.C: A phrase that always makes the subject plural
options.D: A phrase that always makes the subject singular

questions.explanation: An intervening phrase is a phrase placed between the subject and verb that may contain another noun but does not usually change subject-verb agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the agreement rule for a subject followed by 'of + noun'?

options.A: The verb agrees with the noun in the of-phrase
options.B: The verb agrees with the head subject, not the noun in the of-phrase

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the head subject, not the noun in the of-phrase: 'The list of items is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Correct this sentence: 'The quality of the apples are good.'

options.A: The quality of the apples are good.
options.B: The quality of the apples is good.
options.C: The quality of the apples were good.
options.D: The quality of the apples have good.

questions.explanation: The subject is quality, singular, so 'is' is used: 'The quality of the apples is good.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'together with', 'along with' and 'as well as' when they interrupt the subject and verb?

options.A: The verb agrees with the noun after the phrase
options.B: Ignore the added phrase for agreement

questions.explanation: Ignore the added phrase for agreement: 'The teacher, along with the students, is present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for a subject followed by a relative clause?

options.A: The main verb agrees with the relative pronoun
options.B: The main verb agrees with the head subject; the relative-clause verb agrees with the relative pronoun's antecedent
options.C: The main verb is always plural
options.D: The main verb is always singular

questions.explanation: The main verb agrees with the head subject; the relative-clause verb agrees with the relative pronoun's antecedent: 'The boy who lives here is kind'; 'The boys who live here are kind.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule when a prepositional phrase comes between subject and verb?

options.B: The prepositional object does not control agreement

questions.explanation: The prepositional object does not control agreement: 'The bouquet of roses smells sweet.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule with 'one of the + plural noun + who/that'?

options.A: The main verb after 'one of' is usually plural; the relative clause verb is singular
options.B: The main verb after 'one of' is usually singular; the verb in the relative clause agrees with the plural antecedent

questions.explanation: The main verb after one of is usually singular; the verb in the relative clause agrees with the plural antecedent: 'She is one of the students who work hard.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'She is the only one of the students who works hard' and 'She is one of the students who work hard'?

options.A: 'Only one' identifies her as the sole student who works hard (works); 'one of the students' identifies her as a member of a group who work hard (work)
options.B: Both sentences mean the same thing
options.C: The first uses 'work'; the second uses 'works'

questions.explanation: Only one identifies her as the sole student who works hard (works); one of the students identifies her as a member of a group who work hard (work).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'there is' and 'there are'?

options.B: The verb agrees with the real subject that follows

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the real subject that follows: 'There is a book'; 'There are two books.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'there was' and 'there were'?

options.A: Was agrees with a plural subject; were agrees with a singular subject
options.B: Was agrees with a singular subject; were agrees with a plural subject

questions.explanation: Was agrees with a singular subject; were agrees with a plural subject: 'There was a problem'; 'There were problems.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for 'here is' and 'here are'?

options.B: The verb agrees with the subject that follows

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject that follows: 'Here is your file'; 'Here are your files.'

questions.subject: English

questions.explanation: Does is used with he/she/it and singular nouns: 'He does his work.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'has' in the simple present?
questions.explanation: Has is used with he/she/it and singular nouns: 'She has a car.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'am' in the present tense?
questions.explanation: Am is used with I: 'I am ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'is' in the present tense?
questions.explanation: Is is used with he/she/it and singular nouns: 'He is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'were' in the past tense?
questions.explanation: Were is used with you/we/they and plural nouns: 'They were ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'was' in the past tense?
questions.explanation: Was is used with I/he/she/it and singular nouns: 'I was ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a modal verb with a singular subject?
questions.explanation: Modals do not change for singular or plural subjects: 'She can swim.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a modal verb with a plural subject?
questions.explanation: Modals do not change for singular or plural subjects: 'They can swim.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses two singular subjects joined by 'and'?
questions.explanation: Two singular subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: 'Ravi and Rani are friends.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly treats 'bread and butter' as one combined idea?

options.A: Bread and butter are my usual breakfast.
options.B: Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.
options.C: Bread and butter were my usual breakfast.
options.D: Bread and butter have my usual breakfast.

questions.explanation: A singular verb may be used when the words form one unit, one dish, one title or one concept: 'Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'each' before nouns joined by 'and'?

options.A: Each man and each woman have a vote.
options.B: Each man and each woman has a vote.
options.C: Each man and each woman are a vote.
options.D: Each man and each woman were a vote.

questions.explanation: Each before each coordinated singular noun generally takes a singular verb: 'Each man and each woman has a vote.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the poet and novelist' to refer to one person?

options.A: The poet and novelist are attending.
options.B: The poet and novelist is attending.
options.C: The poet and novelist were attending.
options.D: The poet and novelist have attending.

questions.explanation: A singular verb is used when both descriptions identify one person: 'The poet and novelist is attending.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly refers to two people?

options.A: The poet and the novelist is here.
options.B: The poet and the novelist are here.
options.C: The poet and the novelist was here.
options.D: The poet and the novelist has here.

questions.explanation: The article helps show that two people are meant: 'The poet and the novelist are here.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'neither the manager nor the workers'?

options.A: Neither the manager nor the workers is available.
options.B: Neither the manager nor the workers are available.
options.C: Neither the manager nor the workers was available.
options.D: Neither the manager nor the workers has available.

questions.explanation: The verb generally agrees with the subject nearer to it: 'Neither the manager nor the workers are available.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly rewrites an awkward either/or construction?

options.A: Either the manager or the workers is available.
options.B: The manager and the workers are unavailable.
options.C: Either the manager or the workers are available.
options.D: The manager and the workers is unavailable.

questions.explanation: The preferred way to avoid an awkward agreement construction is to rewrite the sentence so that the subjects have the same number: 'The manager and the workers are unavailable.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as well as'?

options.A: The captain, as well as the players, are ready.
options.B: The captain, as well as the players, is ready.
options.C: The captain, as well as the players, were ready.
options.D: The captain, as well as the players, have ready.

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the main subject 'captain': 'The captain, as well as the players, is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'along with'?

options.A: The principal, along with the teachers, are attending.
options.B: The principal, along with the teachers, is attending.
options.C: The principal, along with the teachers, were attending.
options.D: The principal, along with the teachers, have attending.

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the first/main subject: 'The principal, along with the teachers, is attending.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'together with'?

options.A: The students, together with their teacher, is going.
options.B: The students, together with their teacher, are going.
options.C: The students, together with their teacher, was going.
options.D: The students, together with their teacher, has going.

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the main subject 'students': 'The students, together with their teacher, are going.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'in addition to'?

options.A: The clerk, in addition to two assistants, are present.
options.B: The clerk, in addition to two assistants, is present.
options.C: The clerk, in addition to two assistants, were present.
options.D: The clerk, in addition to two assistants, have present.

questions.explanation: The phrase does not change the number of the main subject: 'The clerk, in addition to two assistants, is present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'accompanied by'?

options.A: The officer, accompanied by two guards, were arriving.
options.B: The officer, accompanied by two guards, was arriving.
options.C: The officer, accompanied by two guards, have arriving.
options.D: The officer, accompanied by two guards, are arriving.

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the main subject 'officer': 'The officer, accompanied by two guards, was arriving.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'rather than' in agreement?

options.A: The teacher, rather than the students, are responsible.
options.B: The teacher, rather than the students, is responsible.
options.C: The teacher, rather than the students, were responsible.
options.D: The teacher, rather than the students, have responsible.

questions.explanation: These expressions do not automatically create a compound subject; the verb agrees with the grammatical subject 'teacher': 'The teacher, rather than the students, is responsible.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'except' in agreement?

options.A: All the students, except Ravi, are present.
options.B: All the students, except Ravi, is present.
options.C: All the students, except Ravi, was present.
options.D: All the students, except Ravi, has present.

questions.explanation: These expressions do not automatically create a compound subject; identify the grammatical subject 'students' and make the verb agree with it: 'All the students, except Ravi, are present.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'either' as a standalone subject?
questions.explanation: Either standing alone as a subject is singular in standard formal agreement: 'Either is acceptable.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'neither' as a standalone subject?
questions.explanation: Neither standing alone as a subject is singular in standard formal agreement: 'Neither is correct.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'one of'?

options.A: One of the students are absent.
options.B: One of the students is absent.
options.C: One of the students were absent.
options.D: One of the students have absent.

questions.explanation: The main subject is 'one', so a singular verb is used: 'One of the students is absent.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'each of'?

options.A: Each of the candidates have an identity card.
options.B: Each of the candidates has an identity card.
options.C: Each of the candidates are an identity card.
options.D: Each of the candidates were an identity card.

questions.explanation: Each of takes a singular verb: 'Each of the candidates has an identity card.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'either of' in formal exam grammar?

options.A: Either of the answers are correct.
options.B: Either of the answers is correct.
options.C: Either of the answers were correct.
options.D: Either of the answers have correct.

questions.explanation: Formal exam grammar generally expects a singular verb: 'Either of the answers is correct.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'neither of' in formal exam grammar?

options.A: Neither of the answers are correct.
options.B: Neither of the answers is correct.
options.C: Neither of the answers were correct.
options.D: Neither of the answers have correct.

questions.explanation: Formal exam grammar generally expects a singular verb: 'Neither of the answers is correct.'

questions.explanation: Is treats the family as one unit: 'The family is large.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly focuses on individual members of a family?

options.A: The family is arguing among themselves.
options.B: The family are arguing among themselves.
options.C: The family was arguing among themselves.
options.D: The family has arguing among themselves.

questions.explanation: Are focuses on individual members; British English permits this notional plural agreement more readily: 'The family are arguing among themselves.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'audience' as one unit?

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'jury' as one unit?

questions.explanation: A singular verb is used when the group acts as one unit: 'The class is quiet.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'information' with a count noun?

options.B: Two pieces of information are given.
options.C: Two pieces of information is given.

options.A: A piece of information are useful.
options.B: A piece of information is useful.

options.D: A piece of information have useful.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'a pair of binoculars'?

options.A: A pair of binoculars are on the shelf.
options.B: A pair of binoculars is on the shelf.
options.C: A pair of binoculars were on the shelf.
options.D: A pair of binoculars have on the shelf.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'a pair of spectacles'?

options.A: A pair of spectacles are on the table.
options.B: A pair of spectacles is on the table.
options.C: A pair of spectacles were on the table.
options.D: A pair of spectacles have on the table.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'deer' with a singular meaning?
questions.explanation: The noun has the same singular and plural form, but the verb depends on number: 'The deer is ill' (singular).

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'fish' with a plural meaning?
questions.explanation: The noun has the same singular and plural form, but the verb depends on number: 'The fish are swimming' (plural).

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'economics' as an academic subject?

questions.question: Which sentence correctly emphasises individual coins and uses a plural verb?

options.A: The ten rupees was in separate coins.
options.B: The ten rupees were in separate coins.
options.C: The ten rupees is in separate coins.
options.D: The ten rupees has in separate coins.

questions.explanation: When the individual units or items are emphasised, a plural verb is used: 'The ten rupees were in separate coins.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'one of the + plural noun + who/that'?

options.A: She is one of the students who works hard.
options.B: She is one of the students who work hard.
options.C: She is one of the students who working hard.
options.D: She is one of the students who worked hard.

questions.explanation: The main verb after one of is usually singular; the verb in the relative clause agrees with the plural antecedent: 'She is one of the students who work hard.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the only one of the + plural noun + who/that'?

options.A: She is the only one of the students who work hard.
options.B: She is the only one of the students who works hard.
options.C: She is the only one of the students who working hard.
options.D: She is the only one of the students who worked hard.

questions.explanation: Only one identifies her as the sole student who works hard, so the relative-clause verb is singular: 'She is the only one of the students who works hard.'
